body: RULE: cash is the easiest number to forge, so test that it behaves like cash. (1) YIELD: interest/other income divided by average cash + liquid investments should be near prevailing deposit/T-bill rates (India FDs ~6-8% in most years; US T-bills 0-5%). Satyam's ~Rs 5,000 cr+ 'cash' produced too little real interest; Rs 376 cr of accrued interest was fake. Adjust for mark-to-market funds where gains sit in other income or OCI, and for cash held near year-end only. (2) LOCATION: cash in the company's own name at named banks vs 'trustee', escrow or offshore-subsidiary accounts (Wirecard EUR 1.9 bn in Philippine trustee accounts; Cox & Kings foreign subsidiaries). (3) BEHAVIOUR: holding large cash while also borrowing is irrational unless the cash is trapped, restricted or fake (CLSA on Satyam, Sep 2008: ~$1.2 bn cash yet $56 m of debt). Cash that never returns to shareholders, never funds visible capex and keeps growing with reported profit (not CFO) is a flag. (4) CONSISTENCY: change in cash should reconcile with CFO - capex - dividends. BENIGN WHEN: yield matches market rates, cash is in named banks/AAA instruments, the company returns cash or uses it visibly (Info Edge's large investment book is disclosed by investee and marked to listed prices). TEST: compute yield each year; read the cash note for restricted balances and banks; check gross debt alongside cash.

tests: interest income / avg cash vs market rates

title: When a cash pile is suspect: test its yield, location and behaviour
